title: Artificial Intelligence (AI) in academic research. A multi-group analysis of students’ awareness and perceptions using gender and programme type
extended_summary:
This paper examines whether university students’ awareness of artificial intelligence (AI), their perceptions of AI, and their actual use of AI tools in academic research are related, and whether these relationships differ by gender and programme type. The authors frame the work as addressing a gap in the literature, since prior studies have focused more on AI for instruction and classroom use than on students’ use of AI for research activities such as literature review, summarisation, paraphrasing, plagiarism checking, and data analysis.

The study surveyed 5,554 students from six universities in Nigeria, including undergraduate, master’s, and doctoral-level students. It measured awareness, perception, and utilisation of AI tools such as ChatGPT, Grammarly, QuillBot, Turnitin, Elicit, Consensus, Mendeley, and others. Using exploratory factor analysis, t-tests, structural equation modelling, mediation analysis, and multi-group analysis, the authors tested whether awareness predicted perception and utilisation, whether perception mediated the awareness–utilisation link, and whether these paths differed for male versus female students and undergraduate versus postgraduate students.

The main findings were that students reported high awareness, positive perceptions, and high utilisation of AI tools in research. Awareness positively predicted perception, and both awareness and perception predicted utilisation; perception partially mediated the awareness–utilisation relationship. Subgroup analysis showed notable gender and programme differences: males were generally more aware and more positive in perception, while females reported higher utilisation; postgraduate students were consistently higher than undergraduates on awareness and utilisation. The authors conclude that AI is already widely present in students’ research practices and that curriculum and support strategies should account for differences by gender and academic level when integrating AI into higher education.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed cross-sectional correlational survey with SEM and multi-group analysis, but it is not an intervention study and has no causal design. It provides useful subgroup evidence, but causal credibility is limited and the measures are self-reported.
impact_tier_rationale: The study reports high self-reported use of AI tools and statistically significant subgroup differences, but the practical effect sizes are mostly not reported and the outcome is descriptive rather than demonstrated learning impact. This suggests unclear-to-modest impact on general higher-education research behavior rather than strong educational impact.

interventions.use_case: Survey-based assessment of university students' awareness, perceptions, and self-reported utilisation of AI tools for academic research, including tools such as ChatGPT, SciSpace, Elicit, Consensus, Grammarly, QuillBot, Turnitin, and Mendeley.

finding.finding_summary: Students reported a high level of utilisation of AI tools for academic research (M=20.932, SD=5.67, t(5419)=303.776, p<.001). The paper treats this as evidence that AI tools are widely used to support research tasks such as literature review, paraphrasing, editing, plagiarism checking, and report writing.
finding.measure: Self-reported utilisation of AI tools for academic research
